steps.title: Folders, family trees, and fast search
steps.body:
Your file explorer, a company org chart, a tournament bracket: they are all **trees**. A **binary search tree** keeps smaller values to the left and bigger to the right, so an in-order walk comes out **sorted**.

In five minutes you’ll watch a tree being built and walked recursively, then write the recursive line yourself.

options.why: The root 5 is printed between its left (3) and right (8) subtrees.
Right. In-order visits left, node, right, so a BST comes out sorted.
That’s the insertion order. In-order walks left subtree, node, then right subtree.

steps.title: Trees in four ideas
points: Each node has a value and up to two children, `left` and `right`. The top node is the **root**.
**BST rule**: everything in the left subtree is smaller, everything in the right is bigger.
Trees are naturally **recursive**: a subtree is a tree. Most tree code is "do it for left, then right".
In-order (left, node, right) prints a BST sorted. Search takes **O(height)**.

steps.prompt: A classic trap. What does this print?

options.why: Height counts nodes on the longest path: all four are in one line.
Yes. 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 all go right: a line, not a bushy tree. Unbalanced trees lose their speed.
Each new value hangs below the previous one.
Inserting sorted values sends every node to the RIGHT, so the "tree" is a straight line of 4.

steps.prompt: Your turn. Make count(n) return how many nodes the tree has.
steps.hint: This node counts as 1, plus everything in its left and right subtrees.
steps.explain: `1 + count(n.left) + count(n.right)` counts this node and then lets recursion count each subtree.
